analysis.one_liner: Extends federal regulation to energy derivatives trading and caps speculative positions to prevent energy price manipulation.
analysis.headline: Eleven senators backed the bill, but it never received a committee vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced during the 2008 oil and gas price spike, would have brought energy derivatives—contracts betting on the future price of oil, gasoline, natural gas, coal, and electricity—under regulation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, including trades on foreign exchanges that deliver in the U.S. It would have required uniform limits on how large a position any single trader could hold, voided exemptions that let energy swaps trade without oversight, and required monthly public disclosure of big commodity-index-fund positions. It also gave the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new cease-and-desist and disgorgement powers to protect energy consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households, businesses, and drivers who pay gasoline, heating, and electricity prices. The bill's premise was that unregulated energy derivatives trading could inflate the prices consumers pay at the pump and on their utility bills, and it would have given regulators tools to detect and stop manipulation of those prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households paying gas and heating bills

how_it_helps.text: Extends CFTC regulatory authority to energy derivatives transacted on foreign boards of trade when the delivery point is in the U.S. or the trade is made from a U.S. computer terminal, closing the loophole that allowed such trades to escape oversight [S2][S3].
Requires the CFTC to set uniform limits on the number of energy derivative positions any single person can hold, in all markets combined [S2][S3].

Nullifies CFTC 'no-action letter' exemptions that had allowed energy swap transactions to be conducted without regard to Commodity Exchange Act requirements, and bars new exemptions without 60 days advance notice to Congress and public comment [S2][S3].

Requires the CFTC to publish monthly, on its website, the number and value of long and short positions held by any person in commodity index funds, and the portion that are net long positions in energy transactions [S2][S3].

Gives the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission cease-and-desist and temporary-order authority under the Natural Gas Act and Federal Power Act, including the power to require accounting and disgorgement of improper gains, expressly to prevent significant harm to energy consumers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large traders, swap dealers, hedge funds, and commodity index fund operators in energy derivatives, who would lose the ability to hold unlimited positions and trade without reporting. Commodity exchanges and foreign boards of trade would lose the carve-out for U.S.-delivery energy contracts. There may also be indirect costs to commercial hedgers if tighter limits reduce market liquidity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy derivatives traders and swap dealers

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out 'bilateral' energy transactions from the requirement that trades occur on a regulated exchange, leaving off-exchange trades legal as long as they are reported and records kept for five years—a concession that weakens the bill's own goal of bringing trading onto regulated venues [S3].

The bill's premise—that unregulated speculative trading drove up energy prices in 2008—was contested at the time; if speculation was not a major driver, position limits would impose compliance costs on trading firms without lowering prices for consumers.

Uniform position limits across all markets, and the exclusion of energy swaps from the bona fide hedging exemption, could make it harder and costlier for legitimate hedgers—airlines, truckers, and utilities—to lock in fuel prices, passing costs to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If speculation in unregulated energy derivatives was inflating prices, the bill would have delivered real value to every household that buys fuel and heat, at a cost confined to a concentrated trading industry. But the bill's own bilateral-trade carve-out diluted its reach, and the effectiveness of position limits hinged on an unsettled question about how much speculators actually drove 2008 prices. Honest supporters had to acknowledge the bill might deliver less price relief than its title promised.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in June 2008 and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on June 24, 2008, during the 2008 energy price spike, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S1][S5].
Ten senators—9 Democrats and 1 Independent—signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The committee never held a markup and never reported the bill, and the full Senate never voted on it; the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy derivatives traders, swap dealers, and commodity index funds were better off, because they kept trading without CFTC position limits or the reporting the bill would have required. Energy consumers gained nothing, continuing to pay energy prices without the added regulatory oversight the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy derivatives traders and swap dealers

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to extend CFTC regulation to energy derivatives and impose position limits.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the chamber's only Independent sponsor.

against.name: Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred never held a markup or reported the bill.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the Congress.

against.name: CFTC leadership under President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Had exempted energy swap transactions from Commodity Exchange Act requirements through no-action letters, the very exemptions this bill would void, and opposed extending CFTC jurisdiction and position limits to energy derivatives.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors were Democrats plus one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote in committee or on the floor.

industries.industry: Energy derivatives traders and swap dealers
industries.note: The bill would void the exemptions letting energy swaps trade without oversight, impose uniform position limits across all markets, and require reporting of large bilateral trades, all aimed at curbing speculative influence on energy prices consumers pay [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Commodity exchanges and foreign boards of trade
industries.note: The bill strips these venues of the exemption that let U.S.-delivery energy contracts trade abroad outside CFTC jurisdiction, exposing them to regulation and to the bill's limits on CFTC waivers [S2][S3].

They would gain from a market policed against manipulation, but the bill excludes energy swaps from the bona fide hedging exemption, which could make hedging their fuel costs harder and costlier [S3].
